To expunge something means to remove it completely and permanently — wiping it out so thoroughly that it is as if it never existed in the first place.

It is not a gentle or casual removal. It is total, deliberate, and final. When something is expunged, there is nothing left behind — no trace, no residue, no record.

Think of the difference between crossing something out in a notebook versus shredding the entire page. Crossing out still leaves evidence that something was there. Shredding leaves nothing. Expunging is the shredding.

The word almost always applies to things that are recorded, documented, or stored in some form — a name on a list, an entry in a file, a statement in a document, a memory in the mind. You expunge records, entries, information, passages, and memories. You would not typically use it for physical objects.
Where It Is Most Commonly Used

In legal and official contexts, this is where the word is most at home. The most classic example is expunging a criminal record. If a court expunges someone's criminal record, it officially and permanently erases that conviction from their file. It is no longer visible, no longer accessible, and legally, it is treated as though it never happened. This is a significant and formal act — not just hiding the record, but eliminating it.

In writing and publishing, an editor might expunge a passage from a manuscript — removing it entirely, not just revising it.

In a figurative sense, people say things like "I want to expunge that memory from my mind" — meaning they wish to erase it so completely that it leaves no psychological mark. When used this way, the word carries a sense of great effort and strong intention, because memories, unlike files, are not so easy to delete.

Expunge is a serious, weighty word. It implies that what is being removed is unwanted — something damaging, embarrassing, false, unjust, or offensive. Nobody expunges something they are proud of. The act of expunging always carries the sense of correcting, cleaning, or undoing something.

It also implies authority and effort. You do not casually expunge something. There is usually a deliberate decision — often an official one — behind the act.
How It Differs from Similar Words

This is important, because several words seem close in meaning but are not quite the same.

Delete is the everyday, neutral word. You delete a file, delete a text message. It is ordinary and has no particular emotional weight. Expunge is far more formal, more final, and more loaded with significance.

Erase can be physical (erasing pencil marks) or figurative, but it is softer and less formal than expunge. Erasing suggests removing a mark. Expunging suggests eliminating all evidence of existence.

Remove is the broadest of these words — you can remove almost anything from anywhere. It says nothing about how thoroughly it is done. Expunge specifically implies completeness and permanence.

Purge means to rid something of unwanted elements, often in large numbers (purging a list of inactive members, for example). It can also carry political connotations — a government purging its opponents. Expunge is more precise and targeted; it focuses on one specific thing being wiped out entirely.

Obliterate means to destroy so completely that nothing remains — but it leans more toward physical destruction (a building obliterated by a bomb). Expunge is about records, information, and documentation.

"After serving his sentence and staying out of trouble for five years, he petitioned the court to expunge his criminal record."

"The committee voted to expunge his name from the official registry."

"She desperately wanted to expunge the embarrassing episode from her memory, but it kept coming back."

"Several offensive paragraphs were expunged from the original manuscript before the book was published."

"The organization expunged all references to the disgraced founder from its website and promotional materials."

Expunge is a formal word. You would not hear it in casual everyday conversation — nobody says "I expunged that show from my watch list." It belongs in legal language, official writing, serious journalism, and literary prose. When used outside of legal contexts (like in the memory example), the writer is deliberately reaching for a word that conveys dramatic finality and seriousness.
To expunge something is to erase it completely and permanently from a record, document, system, or memory — with such thoroughness that it is treated as though it never existed.
